blocks.title: Volumetric analysis, indicator and end point
blocks.text: Volumetric analysis finds the concentrations of solutions by titration: a solution of unknown concentration is combined slowly and carefully with a known volume of a standard solution until a colour change shows the completion of the reaction. The substance that indicates the completion of the reaction by its change of colour is the indicator, and the moment at which the indicator changes colour is the end point. Either solution can be taken in the burette, with the other in a conical or titration flask.

Phenolphthalein solution is prepared by adding one gram of the indicator to 500 cm3 of 50% ethanol; only one to two drops are used in 10 cm3 of the solution to be titrated. Its colour changes from pink to colourless as the pH decreases. The light pink colour that marks the end point tends to fade gradually because atmospheric carbon dioxide slowly dissolves in the solution.
Materials: burette, pipette, funnel, conical flask, HCl solution, NaOH solution, phenolphthalein.

items: Rinse the pipette first with distilled water and then with the given NaOH solution.
Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only.
Pipette 10 cm3 of the NaOH solution into the conical flask.
Add one to two drops of phenolphthalein; the solution turns pink.
Rinse the burette first with distilled water and then with the given HCl solution.
Fix the burette upright on a clamp stand.
Fill it with the HCl solution through a funnel, then remove the funnel.
Using the tap at the base, let some acid flow into a beaker to remove any air bubble in the nozzle.
Note the burette reading as the initial reading, using an anti-parallax card or a white paper.
Place the conical flask on a white paper under the burette to see the colour change clearly; check that the burette does not leak.
Carry out a rough titration by adding the acid from the burette dropwise to the flask.
Swirl the contents of the flask while adding acid for thorough mixing.

Keep on adding acid till the colour of the solution becomes light pink persistently: the end point. Note the burette reading as the final reading; final minus initial reading is the volume of acid used.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In this procedure NaOH with phenolphthalein is in the flask (pink) and the acid is added from the burette, so at the end point the pink colour just disappears and the solution becomes colourless (as the book's own box says, pink to colourless as the pH decreases). Step xiii should read: keep adding acid until the pink colour just disappears.

blocks.alt: Five stages: a pipette delivers NaOH solution into a conical flask; a dropper adds indicator and the solution turns pink; a burette of acid shows the initial reading with its tap on hold; the tap is released and acid drops into the pink solution; the final reading is taken with the tap on hold and the flask solution is colourless.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.6: Procedure of titration (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.6).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 16.6 labels the pipette 'Acid solution' and ends with a pink flask, the reverse of the book's procedure. As the procedure says, NaOH is pipetted into the flask, turns pink with phenolphthalein and becomes colourless at the end point, as drawn above.

Repeat the titration to get accurate and concordant readings: at least three concordant readings that agree with one another within 0.1 cm3. The observations are tabulated as rough, 1, 2, 3 with final reading x, initial reading y and volume of acid used (x - y), giving the volume of HCl solution used in cm3.

blocks.title: Molarity equation
blocks.text: M1 V1 / n1 = M2 V2 / n2, where M1, V1 and n1 are the molarity, the volume used and the number of moles in the balanced equation for the acid, and M2, V2 and n2 the same for the base. The molarity of the given base solution is M2 = M1 V1 n2 / (n1 V2).
Define indicator and end point in a titration, and say what is meant by a concordant reading.
